title: COP31: where the world stands, what the UK is doing, and the sticking points
label: 26 October 2026 · COP31 prospects
summary: The UK Special Representative for Climate, Rachel Kyte, told the committee that COP31 will be an "implementation" COP between two stocktakes, framed by scientific warnings that the world is already in overshoot. She outlined priority themes—electrification, methane and other short-lived pollutants, forests, loss and damage, and access to adaptation finance—described how the UK is engaging on forest finance and adaptation leadership, and warned about diplomatic friction over the role of science in the next global stocktake and the political sensitivities around finance and subsidies.

chapters.title: Where we are going into COP31
chapters.takeaway: COP31 is being framed as an "Action Agenda" implementation meeting, with urgency added by scientific findings that the world is already in overshoot.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Rachel, what's your sense of where pre-conference negotiations are and how strong the global position is heading into COP31?

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: This COP sits between the first and the second global stocktake, so it’s a midpoint check on implementation. The opening theme is the Action Agenda—it's about delivery, not new targets.

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: It's also the first COP since scientists said we’re in overshoot, so expect pressure for urgent action and for clearer plans to limit warming and manage impacts.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Do you feel optimistic that the COP will deliver, given it’s an implementation COP rather than a headline negotiation?

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: Cautious optimism. Countries want to keep 1.5°C central and to speed up action: triple renewables, double energy efficiency and move away from fossil fuels. There’s practical focus—grids, interconnectors, electrification, methane cuts, and forests.

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: But big questions remain: how to deliver loss and damage finance at scale, and how to fund resilience—especially before a G20 year with expected severe El Niño impacts.

chapters.title: Who’s still in the room and why it matters
chapters.takeaway: Most parties to Paris remain engaged, but the U.S. absence and political pressures complicate leadership and diplomatic strategy.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You said "no one is turning away"—but the United States has stepped back. How big a problem is that?

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: When I said that, I meant parties still in the Paris process. The US has left the pitch, but 193 other parties remain engaged. The hope among many is that the US could rejoin easily if politics change.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So that leaves 193 countries to make COP31 meaningful?

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: Yes. But agreement on what to do next is not automatic—there’s consensus on goals, less so on who does what to speed change. COP31’s job is to push implementation and constructive coalitions.

chapters.title: UK priorities and the Action Agenda
chapters.takeaway: The UK is promoting multilateral action, electrification targets, methane reduction, forest finance and using its G20 role to improve access to adaptation finance.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What are the UK's priorities at COP31?

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: Defend multilateralism; accelerate the energy transition, including a Turkish priority to reach 35% electrification by 2035; push methane cuts; and operationalise the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF).

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: On finance, the UK wants to use its G20 presidency to tackle debt, prearranged finance and access to adaptation funding so countries can invest in resilience.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Will the Government publish a written ministerial statement on its COP priorities?

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: I don’t know the publication plan offhand; I’ll check. It would be helpful if they did.

chapters.title: Forests and the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF)
chapters.takeaway: The TFFF is an innovative blended-finance attempt to mobilise large-scale funds for forests; structure, governance and fundraising will determine whether it delivers for communities and forests.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: How will the TFFF actually work, and how do we avoid the money not translating into more forests?

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: TFFF is a blended investment vehicle with senior and junior tranches: senior investors expect higher returns, junior investors absorb more risk. Returns will be reinvested, and 20% of proceeds are set to go to indigenous peoples and local communities.

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: The fund sits with a fiduciary vehicle at the World Bank. UK secured a seat on that board and is pushing for a seat on the fund's board. Key tasks now are fundraising, hiring a CEO and CIO, and finalising governance.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: Some worry this is just a financial product—how do we ensure impact for forests and communities?

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: Structure matters. The UK’s involvement as a AAA investor helps crowd in others. If designed and governed well, it could be a new model for funding global public goods; if not, critics are right to be sceptical.

chapters.title: Coalitions, roadmaps and transition support
chapters.takeaway: Informal coalitions and safe spaces like Santa Marta help countries discuss practical transition problems—fiscal, financial and market risks—whereas formal roadmaps suit some countries but not all.

turns.speaker: Dr Roz Savage
turns.text: What are your reflections on the Santa Marta conference and the idea of coalitions of the willing?

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: Santa Marta was valuable: 57 countries used it as a safe, less politicised space to tackle hard transition issues. Coalitions let willing countries move faster without waiting for full consensus.

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: The UK followed up with a Wilton Park meeting inviting developing net-exporting countries to discuss fiscal policy, bond markets and managing stranded assets—issues you won’t usually see debated at a COP plenary.

turns.speaker: Dr Roz Savage
turns.text: Who has published transition roadmaps so far and will the UK publish one?

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: Colombia, France, Germany and the Netherlands have published roadmaps. The UK is still deciding—some of our statutory documents already play that role—while many developing countries prefer practical support over extra documents.

chapters.title: UK credibility, finance, subsidies and climate security
chapters.takeaway: The UK faces questions on delivery of its ambitious NDC, the scale and shape of international climate finance, fossil fuel subsidies, and how to frame climate-related security—while trying to act as a diplomatic bridge.

turns.speaker: Bill Esterson
turns.text: Is there a risk in the UK's ambitious NDC? What would damage credibility if targets are missed?

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: The UK NDC is ambitious but not reckless. Carbon budgets act as guardrails. Missing targets damages credibility and must guide policy, but a transition path can have ups and downs—so we should take it seriously and act.

turns.speaker: Bill Esterson
turns.text: Should we be worried about cuts to heat pump subsidies or loosening zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) mandates?

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: My role is external—bringing global lessons and selling UK credibility abroad. I can't comment on internal ministerial decisions, but other countries watch our choices closely.

turns.speaker: Bill Esterson
turns.text: Does new gas development like Jackdaw hurt our reputation?

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: I don’t think Jackdaw harms reputation; officials have said such projects can be managed within net-zero commitments. I won’t speculate on other projects.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: The UK’s international climate finance (ICF) fell from £11.6bn over five years to £6bn over three; what impact does that have on our standing?

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: The headline fell, but the £6bn is over three years and is complemented by about £6.7bn from non‑ODA instruments—so totals cited reach ~£12.7bn over three years, plus mobilised private finance. The cut to the Green Climate Fund drew particular criticism.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: What about fossil fuel subsidies and joining up biodiversity and climate goals—will the UK get tougher on assessing its own subsidies?

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: That’s a Treasury and G7/G20 discussion. There are active conversations about repurposing subsidies and whether levies could fund resilience for developing countries. UK Treasury officials are engaged in Coalition of Finance Ministers for Climate Action—but I can’t set domestic fiscal policy here.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: On national security: the UK published an assessment of ecosystem collapse risks—what action follows and how will it feature at COP and the G20?

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: The Government moved from assessment to action: a taskforce on climate and nature security meets across Whitehall, a nature security R&D programme has started, and we’ve funded the UN’s climate security mechanism. At COP there will be events, but many countries resist framing climate primarily as a security issue.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: How will the UK leverage its adaptation role with Sierra Leone?

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: Being a co-lead doesn’t mean we’ve solved everything; it’s about diplomatic leadership to help very different countries agree on practical measures for locally led adaptation, financing stacks for resilience, and lessons on heat, floods and prearranged finance.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: The IPCC failed to agree a timetable for its next full assessment—are countries politicising the science?

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: It’s worrying. The Paris process is science-based; not having clear IPCC input for the second stocktake undermines that. There are two reasons for delay: some countries need more support to handle the workload, and some fear the stocktake being used top-down against national sovereignty. Diplomatic work is intense to resolve this.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: Where does the UK stand in that dispute?

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: The UK talks to everyone and acts as a bridge-builder—engaging EU, Arab group, China, India, Brazil, small islands and least developed countries. Our Foreign Secretary is respected on these issues, which helps in convening and mediating.

chapters.title: Concluding view
chapters.takeaway: COP31 can push implementation if countries build the right coalitions, finalise forest finance structures, resolve finance and IPCC process questions, and the UK continues to act as a pragmatic broker.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you, Rachel. We’ll look forward to your post‑COP report—any final words?

turns.speaker: Rachel Kyte
turns.text: Countries want to roll up their sleeves. If COP31 focuses on practical implementation—electrification, methane, forests, access to adaptation finance and loss and damage—it can move the dial. But design, governance and diplomatic care will determine success.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you—safe travels and we look forward to your update on the outcomes.
